title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is one of training-data provenance: an AI music generation system was accused of being built on copyrighted recordings that were used without authorization. This is a data-acquisition failure that occurs before deployment, during the construction of the model itself. Catching it would have required rights clearance at the point of data collection, before any training began, not after the system was already generating music for users.

The legal landscape that followed reflects how unresolved that underlying question remains. Universal Music Group settled and moved toward a licensing arrangement. Warner Music Group did the same. Sony Music filed a separate lawsuit asserting over 30,000 recordings, a figure a judge declined to let Sony add to its original case, prompting a new filing. A class action by independent artists was also allowed to proceed, though moved to a different jurisdiction. A musicians' union brought its own suit over the UMG settlement itself.

None of the lawsuits cited in the reporting have produced a final verdict on whether the training practices were unlawful, and settlements resolve disputes without constituting findings of liability. What is established is that multiple rights-holders disputed Udio's training practices through litigation, that some chose to settle and partner while others escalated, and that the question of what music an AI system may lawfully train on remains unresolved in court.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio by reaching licensing agreements. UMG had accused Udio of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system, which creates original music from text prompts. The settlement includes plans for Udio to launch a new platform next year using only authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize, stream and share their creations. UMG's CEO stated the agreements show their commitment to artists while embracing new technologies and developing new business models. Financial terms were not disclosed.

Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, agreed that artists can participate in the new platform and receive compensation, though specifics remain undisclosed. This marks Udio's first major licensing deal with a record label. The lawsuit had claimed Udio created songs similar to hits like The Temptations' "My Girl" without permission. UMG also announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.
